newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec budget austerity slows separation drive.
newsitem.headline: Quebec budget austerity slows separation drive.

text.p: The need for tough budget cuts has slowed Quebec's drive for independence from Canada, leaving the French-speaking province's separatist government in no hurry to hold another sovereignty referendum.

Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard has vowed to get re-elected with a renewed mandate for separation before trying to call a referendum on the thorny issue. But, while polls show his Parti Quebecois could win handily today, he is not required to call an election until late 1999 and is in no hurry to do so.
Re-election of the Parti Quebecois could mean another referendum on independence in 1999 or 2000.

"Our election will hold the certainty that there will be a referendum afterward," Bouchard said last week as the Quebec legislature adjourned for the summer. He added that he believed Quebec would be a sovereign nation by 2001.
His separatist movement narrowly lost a referendum in October 1995 by 50.6 percent to 49.4 percent. Under Quebec law, a government cannot hold two votes on sovereignty during the same term in office.

Bouchard has several reasons for avoiding an early election and a snap referendum on independence. Vote-weary Quebeckers have gone to the polls in national and provincial elections and referendums in five of the past six years.

Bouchard's debt-ridden government is also implementing a painful austerity programme that seeks to cut C$3.6 billion ($2.6 billion) in costs from its C$40 billion ($29 billion) budget this fiscal year alone. The cuts have led to hospital closings and thousands of layoffs among teachers, health workers and civil servants.

Bouchard has aroused the wrath of some Parti Quebecois colleagues and separatist supporters who accuse him of abandoning the party's social democratic values. Some Parti Quebecois leaders resigned in protest recently, leaving Bouchard on the defensive and forcing him to put his budget plans ahead of the drive for independence.
"It seems Quebeckers need a breather to get used to this new society that is in the process of forming," Bouchard said.

He is pressing ahead with his cost-cutting agenda in a bid to reduce the deficit to C$2.2 billion ($1.6 billion) in fiscal 1997/98 from C$3.2 billion ($2.3 billion) last year, with the goal of balancing the budget by spring 1999.

The Parti Quebecois is also grappling with redefining its independence message to convince voters an independent Quebec would maintain close economic and perhaps even some political ties with Canada. The credibility of this economic partnership proposal is vital for a separatist victory in a referendum.

"The separatists know that a portion of Quebeckers who are tempted to vote for sovereignty will do so only on the condition that Quebec continues to remain part of the Canadian whole in some way through a strong economic partnership," said Claude Gauthier, vice-president of Montreal-based polling firm CROP Inc.
